summary:
Nebo is a web-based blink comparator for NASA's SPHEREx mission. Anyone can fly over the real SPHEREx all-sky infrared map, pick a catalogued target or any position, and see real SPHEREx images from NASA/IPAC IRSA. Preloaded fields open at once, and a new position shows a first preview while it is still being built. Nebo groups the images into observation epochs, co-adds them and renders them on a common grid (north up, 6.15″/px) with a shared brightness scale, so every difference on screen is real. Users blink between epochs, stack them to reveal fainter sources, and overlay ESA Gaia DR3 stars and CatWISE2020 sources, moved to each epoch, to tell catalogued stars from uncatalogued movers. Difference images, RGB composites across the six detectors, measured spectra and community votes help separate real changes from artifacts.

This answers "Planet X and SPHEREx" directly. Faint, cold, nearby objects such as brown dwarfs, or a hypothetical distant planet, give themselves away by moving between SPHEREx visits, which come about every six months. Comparing those visits today takes archive queries, FITS files and Python. Nebo does it in a browser, with nothing to install. It brings to SPHEREx the public approach that found hundreds of brown dwarfs in WISE data, and it only ever talks about observed changes and candidate signals, never discoveries.
details:
What it does and how it works

Nebo is a web blink comparator for NASA's SPHEREx mission. You start in the cockpit of a ship looking at the whole infrared sky. That all-sky map is the real SPHEREx map from IRSA, shown with Aladin Lite. You pick a target, type RA/Dec or move the map, then choose a detector (D1–D6, six bands from 0.75 to 5 µm) and a field size (3′, 6′ or 15′).

For that position, the FastAPI backend works through these steps:

1. It asks NASA/IPAC IRSA which SPHEREx Level 2 images cover the point. It uses TAP, and asks SIA in parallel as a backup when TAP is slow.

2. It downloads cutouts and subtracts the zodiacal light. Pixels flagged as bad are kept out of every measurement.

3. It groups the frames into epochs (SPHEREx revisits the sky about every six months) and co-adds up to 16 frames per epoch, weighting each by its inverse variance.

4. It puts every epoch on a common grid: north up, east left, 6.15″ per pixel. All epochs share one brightness scale, so any change you see on screen is real.

The build runs in stages and shows its progress, and a first preview can already be compared while the remaining frames download. Each finished field is stored in PostgreSQL and reused.

In the field viewer you can:

- Blink between epochs at 0.4, 0.8 or 1.5 seconds per frame.

- Stack epochs to reveal fainter sources.

- See the difference between two epochs: red where the sky got brighter, blue where it got fainter.

- Build false-colour RGB composites from three of the six detectors.

- Overlay ESA Gaia DR3 stars and CatWISE2020 sources, moved to where they were at each epoch.

- Check each epoch's alignment against Gaia stars and show the bad-pixel mask.

The backend also detects changes automatically. It matches the brightness and image sharpness of the first and last epochs, subtracts them and keeps the 5σ residuals. It labels each change as a "catalogued object" or a "candidate signal", and flags residuals on static stars as likely systematics. A "cold candidate" is a source that Gaia doesn't see but that is red in WISE colours (W1−W2 ≥ 1).

On each field's own data, Nebo also measures:

- a 102-channel spectrum, with molecular bands marked (H₂O, CH₄, CO₂, CO);

- a light curve;

- how far the object's centre moved between epochs;

- three hand-tuned models: an event classifier, a spectral-type fit and a forecast. Each is labelled "model estimate, not a detection".

Users can vote on each signal (real change, moving object, artifact, uncertain) and talk in a public chat room for each object.

Benefits and intended impact

SPHEREx data is public, but comparing one patch of sky over time takes archive queries, FITS files, alignment work and Python. Nebo does all of that in a browser, with nothing to install.

Cold, faint, nearby objects give themselves away by moving between SPHEREx visits. These include brown dwarfs, or a hypothetical distant planet. Nebo makes that motion visible to students, teachers, amateur astronomers and citizen scientists. It follows the WiseView model, the blink tool behind the public brown-dwarf searches in WISE data, and adds voting and chat so many people can review each field.

We checked the method on real data. For each featured target, we predicted where it should be in every epoch from its known motion across the sky, then measured where it actually appears in the image. In all 29 epochs where the target was detected, it was within 1 pixel of the predicted spot; the worst offset was 0.64 px (3.9″). The targets are Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855−0714, RW Aurigae and R Draconis.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

- Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, NumPy, Astropy, Pillow, psycopg 3 and PostgreSQL 16.

- Frontend: TypeScript, Next.js and React, Aladin Lite v3 for the sky, Three.js and react-three-fiber with GLSL shaders, GSAP for animation, Tailwind CSS, d3-geo and TopoJSON.

- Data: NASA/IPAC IRSA (SPHEREx TAP, SIA, IBE cutouts, the all-sky map and CatWISE2020) and ESA Gaia DR3, with backup mirrors (GAVO for Gaia, NOIRLab Astro Data Lab for CatWISE) when the main archives are down.

- Deployment: Docker on Google Cloud Run (an API plus a queue worker), an optional Google Cloud Storage cache, and the frontend on Vercel.

- Testing: 221 backend tests (pytest) and 113 frontend tests, plus a Playwright browser journey with axe-core accessibility checks.

- Hardware: none; Nebo runs fully in the cloud and the browser.

- Source code: https://github.com/toroc07/nebo-app

Creativity

Nebo turns a dry archive workflow into a journey. You start in a ship landed on Earth, power it on, warp through a hyperspace tunnel to the cockpit, and turn to the observation room to study each field. The animation lasts only as long as the data takes to load and never covers the science.

It goes beyond the classic blink comparator, with false-colour composites from the SPHEREx detectors, measured spectra, difference images and a 3D hologram of each object, captioned as an illustration.

Factors the team considered

- Scientific honesty: Nebo only talks about "observed changes" and "candidate signals", never discoveries. It keeps catalogued objects apart from uncatalogued ones. Dates and data releases (DR1, QR3) come from the archive, and anything that can't be measured, such as a saturated star, says why.

- Data validity: Nebo never mixes detectors in a comparison. It checks that epochs are aligned using Gaia stars, flags saturation, few frames and crowded fields, and shows the bad-pixel mask.

- Respect for shared archives: IRSA is shared by every team, so Nebo limits parallel downloads, backs off when the archive is busy and caches every result.

- Accessibility: it respects prefers-reduced-motion, lets you adjust the blink speed, and limits rendering quality on small screens.

- Cost and scale: builds run through a queue worker on Cloud Run, and finished images are cached for good.
